analysis.one_liner: Imposes sweeping regulation and advertising bans on tobacco, makes the industry fund public health programs, and limits its lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced, placed on the Senate calendar, and never received a committee or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written the 1997 state tobacco settlement into federal law. It bans most tobacco advertising, outlaws selling tobacco to anyone under 18, puts tobacco under Food and Drug Administration regulation, and requires tobacco manufacturers to pay into a federal fund every year for 25 years to reimburse states for smoking-related Medicaid costs, cover uninsured children, and pay for anti-smoking and quitting programs. In exchange, manufacturers that signed on would get protection from most state and class-action lawsuits, and the payments would be tax-deductible.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teens, through advertising bans, age checks, vending machine bans, and financial penalties on manufacturers if underage smoking does not fall sharply. Smokers who want to quit, through a national cessation program. State governments, through repayment of tobacco-related Medicaid costs. Uninsured children, through new coverage. Tobacco growers and farm communities, through payments for lost quota income and job retraining assistance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Teens, quitters, states, tobacco farm communities

how_it_helps.text: Bans all outdoor tobacco advertising including billboards, outlaws cartoon characters and human images in tobacco ads, prohibits paid product placement in movies and video games, and bars brand-name sponsorship of athletic and cultural events.

Prohibits selling tobacco to anyone under 18, requires photo identification checks, bans vending machines and free samples, and requires states to license every tobacco retailer with escalating penalties and license revocation for repeat sales to minors.

Brings tobacco products under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act as regulated products, with manufacturing standards to reduce harmful constituents including gradual nicotine reduction, and a mandatory 12 milligram tar limit after three years.

Requires tobacco manufacturers to make payments to a National Tobacco Settlement Trust Fund annually for 25 years, funding state reimbursement for tobacco-related Medicaid and treatment costs, health coverage for uninsured children, and a national smoking cessation and public education program.
Imposes financial surcharges on all manufacturers, allocated by market share, if underage tobacco use does not fall by the required percentages.

Requires manufacturers to open their internal research on smoking, health, addiction, and youth marketing to the public through a National Tobacco Document Depository, and terminates the Tobacco Institute and the Council for Tobacco Research.
Pays tobacco quota holders for lost quota revenue and funds transition assistance, community development grants, and college opportunity grants for tobacco farm families.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, who bear the settlement payments, surcharges, licensing and compliance costs, and sharply restricted marketing. Adult smokers, because the bill explicitly requires manufacturers to raise tobacco product prices each year to cover their payments, and cigarette taxes and price increases fall hardest on lower-income smokers. Federal taxpayers also absorb part of the cost, because the bill makes the industry's settlement payments deductible as an ordinary business expense.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers that sign the agreement get immunity from state lawsuits, class actions, and addiction-based claims, and individual injury claims are channeled through restrictive procedures, sharply limiting the public's ability to hold the industry accountable in court.
The bill requires manufacturers to adjust tobacco prices upward to cover their settlement payments, so smokers themselves pay most of the cost, and smokers are disproportionately lower-income.
The industry's payments are made tax-deductible as ordinary and necessary business expenses, shifting part of the cost of the settlement onto federal taxpayers.

The bill forbids any regulation banning tobacco sales simply because tobacco causes disease, and prohibits the elimination of nicotine from tobacco products for 12 years, guaranteeing the industry's existing market while it is being regulated.

It preempts state and local governments from requiring any warning statements beyond the ones the bill specifies, and restricts states' ability to add their own tobacco controls, overriding stricter local rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health gains would have been large: youth-focused advertising bans, real retail enforcement, FDA product regulation, and industry-funded cessation and coverage programs. But the bill was a negotiated deal, and the industry got substantial protections in return: partial lawsuit immunity, a 12-year guarantee against nicotine elimination, a guaranteed market for traditional products, and a tax deduction for its payments. Critics on public health grounds argued it traded away too much legal accountability; critics on industry's side opposed any settlement at all. It is a genuine trade-off, not a clean win for either side.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 1997, placed on the Senate calendar, and sat there without ever getting a committee vote or a floor vote before this Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator John McCain introduced the bill on November 7, 1997, with three bipartisan cosponsors, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders two days later.
No further action was ever recorded: the bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or House consideration before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers were better off: the bill died without a vote, so they avoided its 25 years of settlement payments, advertising bans, FDA product standards, and underage-use surcharges, and kept selling under the weaker rules then in effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco manufacturers, who avoided payments and regulation

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Universal Tobacco Settlement Act to write the 1997 tobacco settlement into federal law.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Majority leadership of the Senate, 105th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought tobacco settlement legislation to a Senate floor vote; the bill sat on the calendar for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Tobacco manufacturers
against.role: Major cigarette and smokeless tobacco companies
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed settlement legislation and funded a large advertising and lobbying campaign against it during 1998.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's four original sponsors split two Republicans and two Democrats, and no floor vote was ever held, so no recorded party split on the bill itself exists; the fight over tobacco settlement legislation in 1998 cut across party lines, with many Republicans resisting the industry payments and some Democrats objecting to the lawsuit immunity.

industries.note: The bill would have charged manufacturers tens of billions over 25 years, imposed surcharges for missed underage-use targets, and regulated their products under the FDA. At the same time it locked in their market: it barred any ban on selling tobacco just because it causes disease, prohibited eliminating nicotine for 12 years, made their payments tax-deductible, and gave signatory companies immunity from state and class-action lawsuits, making them the permanent, protected channel for a legal nicotine product.

The bill pays quota holders for lost quota revenue, funds community development in tobacco-growing regions, and offers workers retraining and college grants, while granting growers and warehouse operators immunity from liability for manufacturers' noncompliance.

industries.industry: Advertising, billboard, and event sponsorship businesses
industries.note: The bill bans outdoor tobacco ads, brand-name sponsorships of sports and cultural events, product placement, and branded merchandise, eliminating a large stream of advertising and sponsorship revenue. That lost revenue is precisely the youth-facing marketing the bill was designed to stop.

industries.industry: Convenience stores and other tobacco retailers
industries.note: Retailers face a new licensing requirement with fees, penalties, and license revocation for selling to minors, plus bans on vending machines, self-service displays, and most point-of-sale advertising, but the bill also keeps tobacco sales legal and maintains their existing product line.
